data.title: Prediction markets herald insider trading risks for private biotechs
data.description:
The entry of prediction markets into the pharmaceutical sector means new pathways to access money, but also brings new risks.

Prediction markets allow users to purchase a stake in the outcome of a given event, ranging from sports events to geopolitical decisions. In May 2026, the two largest prediction market platforms—Kalshi and Polymarket—began offering odds on the outcomes of events in the drug development space.

For example, as of 30 October 2026, Kalshi offers odds on when the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) will approve Eli Lilly’s retatrutide, and Polymarket offers odds on by what date the FDA will approve Moderna’s melanoma vaccine intismeran autogene. Users may bet hundreds of thousands of dollars on the potential outcomes of these events .

Industry commentators have been critical against the incursion of prediction markets into the clinical space. Many have questioned the ethics of financial speculation on potentially life-saving medicines, and the impact of a risk of increased insider trading by those able to use private information to inform their purchases on public prediction market.

Meanwhile, Kalshi stated in May that these odds are intended “to help solve drug development’s information silo problem,” by making this information more available to the public.

In an interview, Chelsea Anderson and Noah Solowiejczyk, partners at the US law firm Fenwick, say prediction markets concerning events in drug development are here to stay. Moreover, even private drug developers could now be exposed to the risk of insider trading. Consequently, developers and regulators will need to adapt to mitigate potential shocks which may be felt in the sector.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Frankie Fattorini (FF): Are Kalshi’s claims that there’s value to including the clinical trials in prediction markets valid? For example, could they offer a new means of information sharing and gauging confidence in drug development programs?

Noah Solowiejczyk (NS): I think there are some countervailing arguments. I know Kalshi has released some statements about this: that making estimates and probabilities on whether certain clinical trials are going to succeed is helpful to the public, and that typically it’s a much smaller universe of individuals that have access to these sorts of estimates about the likelihood of success of a particular clinical trial.

There has also been a lot of criticism that this creates an insider trading risk. I’ve also seen some criticism in the pharmaceutical industry about the possibility that this could distort clinical trials themselves, because companies may be worried that if they see that the market is turning against them, they may pull the plug on a clinical trial early because they’re worried it’s going to affect their stock price.

FF: Chelsea, what do you think about that idea that prediction markets could influence drug development?

Chelsea Anderson (CA): It is challenging, in some respects, to extend the prediction markets into this sphere because it is so technical. It’s not an area in which the normal layperson typically has the expertise to determine what will or will not be successful.

Indeed, a lot of scientists and experts are having difficulties predicting what’s going to be successful. So, I take the idea that opening up these prediction markets to every person is really beneficial for giving an indication of how successful something is going to be with a grain of salt.

We’ve seen this in a lot of different spheres, including in the tech space, where there’s been a rise in these secondary markets and companies are trying to manoeuvre to give people access in different ways.

This ties in some ways to a broader criticism of our capital markets. For a long time there has not been a lot of liquidity and opportunities for individuals to participate in private markets in a way that’s really meaningful. This is in some ways an extension of that, which candidly is probably a fair criticism of the way that our capital markets are set up.

FF: Considering these opposing points, what do you think will be the real impact prediction markets will have on the sector?

NS: I’m speculating, but I’m not convinced that if prediction markets make projections about the likelihood of success of a trial, that folks will start dismissing that and say, this stuff’s so technical that whatever the current going rate is in that market is really irrelevant to me as a private investor.

I tend to think that a public signal will affect things and matter to folks, and it will not be so easy to discount it. Say what you will about prediction markets, but there’s some pretty good data showing that they are a pretty accurate predictors of outcomes in many other areas.

An open question for me is how many event contracts (a binary ‘yes-or-no’ outcome of an event, which pays out depending on that outcome) really are going to be out there at the end of the day, especially when regulators continue to get more educated on this market and think through what kinds of event contracts they want to allow or ban.

You might see a major limiting of the types of prediction market contracts, which the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) will entertain when it comes to [the healthcare] industry if they decide that there are good public policy reasons to do so.

CA: I would just add that part of the challenge is that insider trading is only one component of this. It’s really part of an entire system that’s designed to protect our public capital markets; which is not in place right now on the private side. Without putting that in place, it’s hard to imagine a situation in which the prediction markets are able to trade in a really fair and equitable way.

FF: Are prediction markets here to stay?

CA: My sense is that they’re going to exist in some form. I do think it’s very likely that there’s going to be much more regulation applied and [questions on the] appropriate subjects for bets, but it seems somewhat unlikely that they’re going to go away altogether. It does feel like there’s a high likelihood that the character of them and what’s permitted is going to shift.

NS: I agree. I think they’re here to stay in some form, but what that looks like may change. As regulators get a more nuanced view on this, they may limit what types of markets exist.

data.title: Casgevy gains UK label expansion for younger patient population
data.description:
Vertex Pharmaceuticals and CRISPR Therapeutics have secured a label expansion for their gene editing therapy Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel) from UK regulators – further broadening the drug’s use case across the haematology treatment landscape. 

Through this newfound approval from the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), healthcare providers can now use Casgevy to treat patients with severe sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia aged five and up. This marks a notable expansion in the drug’s UK-based total addressable population, as it was previously only indicated for use in patients aged 12 and up with these conditions. 

While the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) greenlit Casgevy’s use in patients aged 12 and up with both β-thalassemia and sickle cell disease in 2024 and 2025, respectively, it is currently unclear what stance the UK health watchdog will take on its use in patients aged between five and 12. 

Vertex and CRISPR designed Casgevy, a non-viral gene therapy, to target the BCL11A gene to reactivate the production of an oxygen-carrying protein called foetal haemoglobin (HbF) – thus preventing red blood cells from forming their characteristic banana-like shape in sickle cell disease, while improving the functionality of red blood cells in β-thalassemia. 

Casgevy first debuted on global market in 2023 after securing the regulatory greenlight from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of sickle cell disease, with the genetic medicine then netting a second US approval in β-thalassemia in 2024.  

Most recently, the drug was approved by the FDA for use in patients aged two and above – a feat achieved just 53 days post-filing, according to Vertex. 

“Severe sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia are serious, lifelong conditions that in some cases can be fatal,” noted the MHRA’s executive director of operations, Julian Beach, adding that the extension of Casgevy’s utility into a younger patient population was based on “careful assessment of the available evidence” around the therapy’s safety and efficacy. 

Casgevy’s UK label expansion comes as the gene editing therapy continues to establish itself as a potential big seller for Vertex, as it posted revenue growth of 78% and 151% from a quarterly and yearly perspective in Q2 2026.  Currently, analysts at GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, forecast that Casgevy will have a blockbuster future, as they expect the drug to pull in sales of $1.6bn in 2032. 

Cell & Gene Therapy coverage on Pharmaceutical Technology is supported by Cytiva.

Editorial content is independently produced and follows the highest standards of journalistic integrity. Topic sponsors are not involved in the creation of editorial content.

data.title: Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide outperforms big pharma companies in Q3
data.description:
Eli Lilly posted another strong quarter fuelled by its obesity franchise medications, with company revenue soaring 39% compared to Q3 in 2025.

Lilly has become the dominant big pharma company in recent years, and its quarterly performance showed no signs of letting up.  Tirzepatide brands Mounjaro and Zepbound predictably provided much of the financial firepower, with the type 2 diabetes and obesity medications generating $10.7bn and $5.4bn in global sales, respectively.

Tirzepatide’s total quarterly take-home of around $16.1bn meant the drug outperformed the total revenue of many other big pharma companies in Q3, including Novartis, GSK, and Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), among others.

Lilly’s Q3 performance also reflects how it is accessing more of the cardiometabolic market compared to last year. Mounjaro’s sales were up 65%, while Zepbound grew 59%. Lilly’s Q3 revenue growth of 39% was lower than the 48% from Q2, though this was largely down to pricing pressures.

Still, the metrics were enough for Lilly to once again raise its full-year outlook. The drugmaker now expects total 2026 revenue of between $91bn and $92bn, up from the $85bn to $87bn as previously earmarked. The latest uplift means Lilly has now raised its guidance in every quarter so far this year.

In a research note, Citi analysts called it: “Another exceptional quarter. We continue to see robust growth that remains unparalleled among its peers.”

Lilly is also duking it out with Novo Nordisk in the oral glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) arena, a modality seen as another fueller of the weight loss market. While Novo has raced to market its Wegovy pill in the US, Europe, and the UK first, Lilly is leaning on easier administration of its Foundayo (orforglipron) pill to close the gap.

With further international Foundayo launches expected next year and buoyed by a wider pipeline that has seen several key approvals this year – such as breast cancer drug Inluriyo (imlunestrant) – analysts only see positive momentum for Lilly.

“Altogether, Lilly’s volume momentum, expanding access, portfolio breadth, and successful commercial execution support industry-leading growth reinforce its position as our favourite large biopharma,” the analysts at Citi said.

With positive momentum, Lilly is ensuring it maintains a diverse portfolio. The company has undertaken a swathe of M&As this year. Recent deals include an up to $2.9bn takeover of autoimmune drug developer Merida Biosciences in August and the purchase of psychedelics specialist AtaiBeckley for $2.8bn in July. Lilly has also outlaid billions of dollars into bolstering its manufacturing footprint in the US and Europe to keep up with medicine demand.

Lilly’s pipeline has strong assets moving forward, too. Retatrutide, a triple glucagon agonist, is at the forefront of late-stage assets. The drug has demonstrated strong weight loss in Phase III trials, and outperformed Novo’s Ozempic in a trial readout earlier this week.

data.title: Glenmark opens Allentown distribution hub in US
data.description:
Glenmark Pharmaceuticals has inaugurated an approximately 160,000ft² distribution hub in Allentown, Pennsylvania, US, consolidating all of its American shipping operations into a single location.

Set across a 6.5-acre site, the facility functions as the company’s sole distribution centre in the US.

A workforce of 45 members handles administration, quality control, and general operations at the premises. These employees dispatch both over-the-counter and prescription pharmaceuticals to 321 destinations situated across 43 states.

Since it began operating, the facility has distributed in excess of 61 million units nationwide.

Glenmark Pharmaceuticals president and North America business head Marc Kikuchi said: “Glenmark has served US patients for more than two decades, and we continue to invest in the people and capabilities that enable us to serve patients, customers and partners across the country.

“Our growing US platform spans innovation, manufacturing and distribution, and the Allentown distribution centre is an important part of that commitment. We chose the Lehigh Valley for its exceptional workforce, strong community, and proximity to our customers and US headquarters.

“We are proud to operate a central distribution hub that helps keep Glenmark’s medicines moving to patients nationwide from right here in the Lehigh Valley.”

The facility conforms to regulatory standards set by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

Its technical specifications feature cold-chain refrigerated areas, controlled-room-temperature sections, and DEA-compliant vaults and cages.

Operational practices at the property incorporate adjusted packaging, energy-efficiency initiatives, recycling, reduced waste, refined delivery routes, and specific protocols for shelter-in-place events, evacuations, and medical emergencies.

Across the US, Glenmark employs nearly 400 individuals and manages a portfolio of 229 FDA-authorised products that account for 90 million domestic prescriptions each year.

The company has directed close to $1bn into domestic manufacturing and research infrastructure, which includes almost $400m allocated to an FDA-cleared manufacturing site in Monroe, North Carolina.

The Allentown facility complements Glenmark’s other American properties, comprising its Elmwood Park corporate headquarters in New Jersey and Ichnos Glenmark Innovation, a wholly owned biotechnology subsidiary based in New York.

data.title: Dren Bio raises $350m for dibotatug clinical development
data.description:
Dren Bio has secured $350m in an oversubscribed private financing round to advance its primary investigational therapy, dibotatug (DR-01), via late-stage clinical evaluation, regulatory submission, and potential commercialisation.

The privately held clinical-stage biotechnology company will also use the capital to progress its broader research pipeline in autoimmune disorders, immunology, neurology, and oncology.

Juvia Group and Lightspeed Venture Partners co-led the investment round.

Following the transaction, Juvia Group co-founder and managing director Sujal Shah and Lightspeed partner Shelley Chu have joined the Dren Bio Board of Directors.  

Additional new participants included Cormorant Asset Management, General Catalyst, Mirae Asset Capital Life Science, and OrbiMed.

Existing investors 8VC, Aisling Capital, ArrowMark Partners, BVF Partners, HBM Healthcare Investments, Mission BioCapital, SR One, and Taiho Ventures also contributed capital.

Dibotatug is a fully human monoclonal antibody engineered to bind cluster of differentiation 94 (CD94). The therapy selectively removes disease-causing cytotoxic cells whilst sparing the wider immune system.

The company’s furthest advanced clinical programmes focus on cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma, an aggressive haematologic malignancy, and large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, a chronic condition associated with severe neutropenia, anaemia, and transfusion requirements.

Neither disease currently has approved therapeutic options.

More than 300 individuals have received treatment in an ongoing Phase I/II trial evaluating dibotatug for relapsed or refractory forms of both conditions.

Dren Bio plans to expand clinical testing of dibotatug into aplastic anaemia, other bone marrow failure syndromes, and autoimmune indications.

Dren Bio CEO and founder Nenad Tomasevic said: “We founded Dren Bio with a simple vision: pursue novel science to develop medicines that meaningfully improve the lives of patients with devastating diseases and few treatment options.

“Seeing dibotatug advance to this late stage of development, alongside a clinically validated platform that continues to generate promising new therapies, is deeply gratifying and reflects the vision that inspired us from day one.”

In July 2024, Dren Bio partnered with Novartis subsidiary Novartis Pharma to discover and develop therapeutic bispecific antibodies to treat cancer.

data.title: RFK Jr backs compounding of six unapproved peptides in new policy
data.description:
US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr (RFK Jr) has debuted a policy that allows specific licensed professionals to use a range of unapproved wellness peptides in compounding. 

Through RFK Jr’s Enforcement Discretion Policy, pharmacists, licensed physicians or outsourcing facilities under the direction of a licensed pharmacist will now be able to use six active peptide bulk drug substances when creating compounded drugs – despite none of them having secured a regulatory greenlight from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).  

Under the new policy, HHS will allow for the compounding of BPC-157, a peptide focused on bone healing, as well as anti-ageing and insomnia-focused compound, Epitalon, anti-inflammatory and immune-boosting peptide, KPV, metabolism-regulating MOTS-c, cognition-enhancing Semax and exercise recovery-focused molecule, TB-500. Currently, a lion’s share of the data behind the effectiveness of these drugs is derived from preclinical studies, while little is known about their activity in humans.  

The HHS’ new policy echoes the recommendation of the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee’s (PCAC) July recommendation to allow compounding with these six peptides, despite FDA staff at the agency’s drug evaluation centre taking an opposing stance.  

Unapproved peptides head to the mainstream 

RFK Jr’s call to ink the Enforcement Discretion policy marks another step by the health secretary to legitimise and improve the availability of wellness and longevity-focused peptides across America.  

While these unapproved drugs have traditionally remained on the fringe of the wider health and wellness movement, they are now gaining notable cultural relevance – with peptide combinations like BPC-157 and TB-500, colloquially known as the Wolverine stack, becoming increasingly embedded into the mainstream consumer market. This trend is primarily driven by the soaring popularity of wellness influencers active on social media platforms. 

According to researchers from the University of Queensland’s School of Public Health, there were more than 130,000 posts on Instagram focused on peptide-related content as of May 2026, while videos on the topic garnered more than 230 million views on TikTok at the same time point. 

Reacting to HHS’ new policy, the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies’ (ASOP) board chair and former FDA drug security, integrity and response director, Dr Leigh Verbois, said: “Expanding access is not a substitute for evidence of safety and effectiveness, nor is it a solution to the illegal online market.”  

“Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and a policy of enforcement discretion does not establish that these peptides are safe or effective. Policymakers must maintain evidence-based safeguards while taking meaningful action against illegal online sellers that put consumers at risk.” 

ASOP also warns of the swirling illicit online peptide market, which they say could put patients at significant risk due to its unregulated nature – a possibility it says could be further exacerbated by inviting new market entrants following the debut of the Enforcement Discretion policy. 

In recent months, the FDA has cracked down on the sales of online, black market weight loss peptides, while pharma companies like Eli Lilly also launch their own initiatives to curb the impact of the illicit medicines trade.

Unlike Verbois, the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding’s CEO, Scott Brunner, was generally positive about the policy development, noting it as “an important step for patients.”

“We’ve said all along that the question isn’t whether patients are using these peptides – they are,” Brunner commented, adding that allowing state-licensed pharmacies to prepare these medications “pursuant to legitimate prescriptions, using appropriately sourced and tested API” offers as safer alternative to current sources.

However, he caveats that access must come with meaningful safeguards. “That’s why APC has consistently advocated guardrails focused on API quality and traceability, serious adverse event reporting, and utilisation data,” said Brunner.

“We’re encouraged that the HHS policy addresses those priorities, including requiring API from FDA-registered manufacturers, verification and review of certificates of analysis, extensive testing and documentation, and reporting of serious adverse events and product quality issues,” Brunner concluded.

data.title: Podcast: ESMO26: Major readouts from the 2026 congress
data.description:
This year’s European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress has come to a close, with hundreds of studies having been presented.

The congress, which took place in Madrid, Spain, from 23 to 27 October, featured the first data presentation for MSD and Moderna’s intersimran autogene, a cancer vaccine which met its primary endpoint in a Phase III melanoma study. The data was leaked two days ahead of the Presidential Symposium due to an embargo breach, which shocked journalists and delegates alike on the ground.

A key theme of the conference this year was the continued rise in use of targeted therapies in earlier lines of treatment, with chemotherapy seemingly being phased out in both hot and cold tumours in the first line of treatment – something which one expert told Pharmaceutical Technology‘s sister publication Clinical Trials Arena he would never have believed if he had heard just a few years ago.

Another key theme, highlighted by a GlobalData analyst, was China’s rise in innovative medicines, with five of the 12 late-breaking abstracts (LBAs) being China-originated therapies.

Listen below to our ESMO special edition podcast, featuring commentary from editor Abigail Beaney and analysts Jasminemay Barcelon and Artem Naumenko, who were all on site in Madrid this year, as well as Annabel Kartal-Allen, reporter for Clinical Trials Arena, for all of the biggest study readouts, as well as the key themes that came from the 2026 congress.

You can listen to more podcasts from the GlobalData Media Healthcare team here.

data.title: UK Budget light on life sciences but more doors open for biotech startups
data.description:
The UK Autumn Budget offered little in the way of new measures specifically for the life sciences sector, though incentives for early-stage businesses could help certain biotechs looking to establish themselves in Britain.

At the heart of the government’s aim is a new tax relief for founders looking to scale their companies in the UK. Called “Founders Relief”, the framework will offer eligible founders of high-growth, innovative companies a reduced 10% rate of Capital Gains Tax on up to £10m of lifetime gains. This marks a steep markdown from the standard rate of 18%.  There are several scaling, innovation, and business activity criteria that need to be met for a founder to qualify for the scheme.

Reacting to the Budget, BioIndustry Association (BIA)’s CEO Chris Molloy said: “Although there is broad merit in the Founders’ Relief, the initial inclusion criteria are more relevant to high street businesses, not high-tech, VC-backed biotechs. We shall be working with members and Treasury during the next month’s consultation period to ensure the needs of biotech founders are well understood.”  

Gail Vallis, corporate and life sciences partner at law firm Gardner Leader, disagreed, commenting: “This is great news for those taking substantial risks in setting up promising new companies, especially at the cutting edge of R&D in areas such as life sciences, but misses the mark for those who have taken the same risks on an existing early-stage company or those that have saved a struggling business. It will be very interesting to see what the qualifying conditions will be for a company to be considered high growth or innovative.”

Alongside the relief, people starting a business will have their trading allowance tripled to £3,000. The government said it would also improve venture capital (VC) schemes and simplify access to R&D tax reliefs, as well as making it easier for employees to own shares in the companies they work for.    

Chancellor John Healy announced a £20.4bn boost to the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank (BBB). The latter is a key financing vehicle for British small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Molley said: “We are pleased to see the Chancellor fuel the life sciences innovation engine through an increased and front-loaded budget for BBB that will back funders and companies across biotech and dual-use technologies.”

This Budget also brings new legislation to make non-compete clauses less of a barrier for startups and scaling firms to attract talent, with guidance slated for release in early 2027.

The government said the steps will help achieve its ambition in making the UK “the best place in the world to start a business, scale it, and stay here for the long term”.

One of the few life science-specific announcements was a series of public-private investments worth over £1bn, though only £70m of this was backed by government grants. US biopharma Vertex Pharmaceuticals is opening a new £300m facility in Oxford, medtech specialist Convatec is investing over £500m over the next decade in a new R&D hub in Manchester, and CDMO Kindeva is pumping £200m at its base in Loughborough.

Vallis commented: “£70m of grant funding is fantastic too, but that won’t go far for companies looking to take their drugs through clinical trials. Work is still required to attract investors to invest more widely across the sector.”

The Budget comes at a time of renewed hope in the UK’s biotech sector. A report released this week by the BioIndustry Association (BIA) has found that the UK is likely on track to post its best year since 2021 for biotech VC acquisition.

As the British life sciences funding scene looks to get back to winning ways, M&A has already seen notable success so far this year, with three acquisition deals above $1bn of British biotechs in 2026. The most expensive of these was Eli Lilly purchasing sleep drug biotech Centessa Pharmaceuticals for up to $7.8bn in June. However, the wait for a biotech listing in the UK this year goes on, reflecting hesitancy around the nation’s wider macroeconomic health.

data.title: Enthorin and Rumi sign agreement for FXS therapy
data.description:
Enthorin Therapeutics has signed an option-to-license agreement with Rumi Therapeutics to advance ENT-7340 for Fragile X syndrome (FXS), as well as other intellectual and developmental disabilities.

Under the deal, Rumi Therapeutics will develop the therapy, renaming it RTX-7340.

Enthorin Therapeutics will receive an upfront sum, an option exercise fee, and milestone payments.

The company is also eligible for further payments linked to development, regulatory, and commercial targets, alongside royalties on future net product sales.

It will also contribute scientific and technical expertise to assist during the initial stages of the work.

ENT-7340 is an investigational new drug (IND) enabled small molecule that selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A).

It controls cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and cyclic guanosine monophosphate signalling pathways (cGMP), which influence neuronal function and synaptic plasticity.

FXS is an inherited neurodevelopmental disorder stemming from Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) gene alterations that reduce or prevent the generation of functional FMRP, a protein essential for brain development.

The condition causes varying degrees of cognitive, behavioural, linguistic, and sensory difficulties in both males and females.

Enthorin Therapeutics co-founder and chief scientific officer Marco Peters said: “ENT-7340 represents years of discovery and development work aimed at translating the biology of PDE2 inhibition into effective therapeutics for the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders such as Fragile X.

“Rumi brings distinctive capabilities for evaluating therapeutics in human cellular and organoid models, providing an opportunity to further validate the biology of RTX-7340 in human systems and explore its mechanism of action in FXS and additional indications.

“We are excited about this agreement and look forward to supporting Rumi during the initial development phase as they advance the programme toward clinical development.”

Rumi Therapeutics, an operating company under parent firm Rumi Holdings alongside Rumi Scientific, plans to advance the therapy into clinical testing by drawing on human organoid disease models.

Enthorin Therapeutics developed the programme with research support from the FRAXA Research Foundation.

data.title: Formation Bio launches $600m drug development fund
data.description:
US-based AI-focused pharmaceutical company Formation Bio has launched the Formation Bio Drug Development Accelerator Fund with a capital of $600m aimed at broadening the company’s clinical-stage medicines portfolio.

The initiative will support the acquisition and clinical advancement of ten to 15 drug programmes over the next three to five years.

The company plans to source Phase I and Phase II assets from biotechnology and pharmaceutical entities through acquisitions or in-licensing agreements.

Selection prioritises therapies addressing conditions with substantial unmet need and limited industry development, focusing on programmes with clear pathways to clinical proof of concept.

Formation Bio aims to reach major clinical milestones within two to four years of acquiring each asset, before pursuing commercialisation or co-commercialisation agreements with pharmaceutical partners.

Capital from the vehicle will be deployed through a hub-and-spoke operational model, with each funded programme housed within an independent corporate entity.

Formation Bio serves as the fund’s general partner via a wholly owned subsidiary and has invested its own capital alongside external limited partners.

These backers include hospitals, institutional endowments, philanthropic organisations, and research foundations.

Formation Bio co-founder and CEO Benjamine Liu said: “This fund gives our LPs access to an important and emerging investment category—individual drug assets—through a capital-efficient structure.

“For Formation Bio, it expands the number of promising drugs we can pursue, gives us strategic and financing flexibility, creates paths to liquidity without selling the parent company, and positions us to lower our cost of capital over time.

“Together, these advantages address structural challenges in our industry, allow us to develop more drugs for patients, and support our ambition to build this generation’s enduring pharma company.”

Formation Bio has its headquarters in New York City and a second office in Boston. It combines computational platforms with clinical trial operations to progress drug candidates.
